meta.blurb: The best general never has to fight. That is the strange claim of a book written about 2,500 years ago in China and credited to Sun Tzu. It says to win first, through planning, timing and knowing yourself and your rival.
meta.bible: Sun Tzu: the thinker and general traditionally credited with the book; scholars disagree about who he was and when the text was finished. The Art of War: an ancient Chinese book of strategy in thirteen chapters, written about two and a half thousand years ago. China: the land of the Warring States. Wu and Yue: two old rival states of that region. Chapters in order: Laying Plans, Waging War, Attack by Stratagem, Tactical Dispositions, Energy, Weak Points and Strong, Maneuvering, Variation in Tactics, The Army on the March, Terrain, The Nine Situations, The Attack by Fire, The Use of Spies. Five factors: the way, heaven, earth, the commander, method. Five kinds of spies: local, inside, double, doomed, living. Key terms: Strategy, Stratagem, Commander, Deception, Siege, Morale, Terrain, Spies. Voice and tone: calm, clear and wise, like a teacher; the book is about avoiding war and winning wisely; fighting is treated factually and without gore; ideas are credited to the book and its tradition, never invented.

Sun Tzu says war is very serious, because people can die.
Sun Tzu says we must think about five things before a war.
The first thing is the way: the people trust their leader.
Heaven means the weather, the seasons, and the time of day.
Earth means the land: near or far, flat or steep.
A good leader is wise, honest, kind, brave and strict.
Method means the army has good order and enough food.
Sun Tzu compares the two armies and counts who is stronger.
Sun Tzu says war is often a game of tricks.
We make the enemy think we are far when we are near.
War costs a lot of money, and the farmers pay for it.
A long war makes the soldiers tired and the country poor.
Sun Tzu says a quick win is better than a long fight.
A smart army takes food from the enemy.
Good leaders treat the people they catch with kindness.
The best win is the one with no fighting at all.
First stop the enemy's plans, and only later fight his soldiers.
Attacking a city is the worst way to fight.
A wise leader wins a city without a long fight.
Sun Tzu gives five signs that show who will win.
A king far away should not give every order to his army.
Know the enemy and know yourself, and you will win.
First, we must make ourselves very hard to beat.
When we are weak, we defend, but when we are strong, we attack.
The best winners make winning look easy.
A winning army makes its plan first and fights second.
With good order, a big army moves like a small one.
Direct and surprising moves can be mixed in many ways.
Good timing gives an army great power, like rushing water.
Wait for the enemy to come to you, and be rested.
Strike where the enemy is not ready to defend himself.
A good leader hides his plans so well that nobody can read them.
Water has no fixed shape, and a good army is like water.
The hardest thing in war is to make a long road short.
If soldiers hurry too much, they become tired and fall behind.
An army should be fast like the wind and still like a mountain.
An army is strongest in the morning and weaker at night.
A wise leader knows when to change the rules.
A wise leader looks at both the good and the bad.
A bad temper and fear can ruin even a good general.
Birds that suddenly fly up from trees can show hidden men.
A leader who cares for his soldiers will be followed.
Soldiers with no way out will fight very hard.

B1B2: The Art of War is one of the oldest books about strategy in the world. It is credited to Sun Tzu, a Chinese thinker who lived about two and a half thousand years ago.
Sun Tzu begins by saying that war is a matter of life and death for a country. It can lead to safety or to ruin, so it must never be entered carelessly.
Sun Tzu names five things that decide a war: the way, heaven, earth, the commander and method. A wise leader must study all five carefully before he decides anything at all.
The way means that the people and their ruler share the same goal. When they do, the people will follow him through danger without fear.
Heaven means everything that time and weather bring: day and night, heat and cold, and the changing seasons. A good leader chooses the right time to move his army.
Earth means the shape of the land, which may be near or far, open or narrow, safe or dangerous. Whoever knows the ground well fights with a great advantage.
The commander must have five qualities: wisdom, honesty, kindness, courage and strictness. Without them, even the best plan will fail in his hands.
Method is the way an army is organised, with clear ranks, firm rules and a steady supply of food. A well-run army is much harder to defeat than a muddled one.

Sun Tzu asks seven questions about both sides, such as which ruler is wiser and which army is better trained. He says that the leader who does the most careful counting before the battle is the one who usually wins.
Sun Tzu says that all warfare is based on deception. When you are strong, you should look weak, and when you are ready, you should look unprepared.
Make the enemy believe that you are far away when you are near, and near when you are far. Offer him a small prize so that he walks into a trap.
In his chapter on waging war, Sun Tzu counts the cost of an army in the field. Every day of marching costs a great deal of money, and ordinary families have to pay for it.
When a war lasts too long, weapons grow dull and soldiers lose heart. Then neighbouring rulers see a weak country and decide to attack it.
Sun Tzu says that a quick, plain victory is better than a long and clever one. Speed saves money, lives and the strength of the army.
Sun Tzu advises an army to feed itself from the enemy's land. Carrying food over long roads is so expensive that one load taken from the enemy is worth many loads from home.
Sun Tzu says that captured soldiers should be treated well and, if possible, taken into your own army. In this way, he says, a victory makes you stronger instead of weaker.
In his chapter on attack by stratagem, Sun Tzu says that the best result is to take a country whole and unharmed. To win a hundred battles is good, but to win without fighting at all is better still.
Sun Tzu lists four ways to fight, from best to worst. The best is to ruin the enemy's plans, then to break his alliances, then to attack his army, and last to attack his cities.
A siege takes months and costs many lives, and the walls often stay standing. Sun Tzu says that attacking a walled city is a last choice, used only when there is no other way.
A skilled leader makes the enemy give up without a siege and ends a war without a long campaign. His victory is so quiet that few people even notice it.
Sun Tzu lists five signs of victory, such as knowing when to fight and when not to fight. The winner also has an army that is united and a ruler who does not interfere.

Sun Tzu warns that a ruler can harm his own army by giving orders from far away. If he commands the army to move or stop at the wrong moment, the officers become confused and the enemy takes advantage.
Sun Tzu gives his best-known advice: know your enemy and know yourself. If you know both, you need not fear a hundred battles, but if you know neither, you will lose every time.
In the chapter on tactical dispositions, Sun Tzu says that a good commander first makes himself impossible to defeat. Then he waits for the moment when the enemy can be beaten.

Sun Tzu says that a leader should defend when he lacks strength and attack when he has plenty. A good defender hides like someone deep underground, and a good attacker strikes like lightning from the sky.
Sun Tzu says that seeing a victory everyone can see is no great skill. The best fighters win so easily that people never think of them as heroes.
The winning army wins first and goes to battle afterwards. The losing army goes to battle first and only then hopes to find a way to win.
In the chapter on energy, Sun Tzu says that a large army can be managed as easily as a small one. The secret is good organisation and clear signals, such as drums by day and flags by night.
Sun Tzu says that there are two kinds of moves in war: the direct and the surprising. They can be combined in endless ways, just as five musical notes can make countless songs.
Sun Tzu compares a well-timed attack to a stream that carries stones along with it. Power, he says, comes from gathering energy and releasing it at exactly the right moment.
In his chapter on weak points and strong, Sun Tzu says that the leader who arrives first on the battlefield waits at ease. The one who arrives later must hurry, and he comes already tired.
A good army strikes at places that the enemy has left unguarded. A good defender is so hard to read that the enemy does not know where to attack.
Sun Tzu says that a great commander is mysterious and has no fixed shape. The enemy cannot guess his plans, so he cannot prepare for them.

Sun Tzu compares an army to water, which flows downhill and takes the shape of the ground. A smart leader avoids the enemy's strength and attacks his weakness, and changes his plans as the situation changes.
In the chapter on maneuvering, Sun Tzu says that the hardest task is to turn a long road into a short one. A clever general sets out later than the enemy and still arrives first, by tricking him.
Sun Tzu warns that hurrying an army without rest is dangerous. The strongest soldiers arrive first and the weakest fall behind, and an army without supplies cannot survive.
Sun Tzu uses an old saying to describe how an army should act. It should be swift as the wind, quiet as a forest, fierce as fire and unmoving as a mountain.

Sun Tzu says that an army's spirit is sharpest in the morning, weaker at midday and gone by evening. A wise general avoids the enemy when his spirit is high, and never corners a desperate enemy who has no way out.

In the chapter on variation in tactics, Sun Tzu says that a general must know when to ignore the usual rules. There are roads not worth taking, armies not worth attacking and orders that must not be obeyed.
Sun Tzu says that a wise leader always weighs both the advantages and the disadvantages of a plan. By doing this, he can find a way out of trouble and keep a good plan from turning into a mistake.
Sun Tzu lists five faults that can ruin a general. They are being reckless, being a coward, having a quick temper, caring too much about his own honour and worrying too much about his men.

In the chapter on the army on the march, Sun Tzu advises camping on high ground near water. He also teaches soldiers to read signs, for example birds rising suddenly from a wood, which can show that enemy soldiers are hiding there.

In the chapter on terrain, Sun Tzu says that a commander who treats his soldiers like his own children will be followed anywhere. But kindness alone is not enough, because soldiers who are never corrected become like spoiled children.
In the chapter on the nine situations, Sun Tzu says that soldiers fight hardest when there is no way to escape. Facing a real danger, they find a strength they never knew they had.
Sun Tzu says that a good army should move like a snake: strike its head and the tail answers. He adds that even enemies from Wu and Yue helped each other when they were in the same boat in a storm.

In the chapter on the attack by fire, Sun Tzu describes how fire can be used against an enemy camp. He says that fire needs the right season and the right weather, such as a dry time with a strong wind.
Sun Tzu says that no ruler should start a war because he is angry. A man who is angry can become happy again, but a country that is destroyed cannot return.

In the last chapter, on the use of spies, Sun Tzu says that knowledge of the enemy cannot come from guesses or from spirits. It must come from people who know, and paying them costs far less than a long war.
Sun Tzu names five kinds of spies: local, inside, double, doomed and living. He says they must be rewarded generously and their work must be kept absolutely secret.

The Art of War is still read today by soldiers, teachers, athletes and business people. Its main lesson is that careful thinking and preparation matter more than force, and that the best victory is the one that avoids a battle.
C1C2: The Art of War is a short Chinese book on strategy, and it has been read for roughly two and a half thousand years by generals, rulers and, more recently, business leaders and athletes. Tradition credits it to Sun Tzu, a military thinker of the ancient Chinese states, although scholars still argue about who he was and exactly when the text took its present form. Whatever its origins, it endures because its subject is not really fighting at all, but the clearer thinking that lets a person avoid a fight, or win it cheaply.

Sun Tzu opens his book with a warning: war is the greatest affair of a state, the ground on which lives are saved or lost and a nation either survives or vanishes. For that reason, he insists, it can never be left to impulse, pride or anger, but must be examined from every side. A ruler who goes to war without first studying it deeply is gambling with the lives of everyone he governs.

Sun Tzu says that every war rests on five factors, which he calls the way, heaven, earth, the commander and method. A ruler who understands all five has already done half the work of winning, and one who ignores even a single factor is moving blindly. Each of them, as the next pages show, is a question that must be answered honestly before a single soldier marches.

By the way, Sun Tzu means the bond of shared purpose between a ruler and his people. When the ruler is just and the people believe in him, they will follow him into danger as though they had no fear of death. An army that fights for something it believes in has an advantage that no amount of cleverness elsewhere can replace.

Heaven, in Sun Tzu's language, covers all that belongs to time and the sky: night and day, cold and heat, and the slow turning of the seasons. An army that marches in the wrong season may be beaten by the weather before it ever meets an enemy. A wise commander therefore reads the calendar as carefully as he reads a map.

Earth is the third factor, and it takes in distance, height, breadth and every kind of ground, from open plains to narrow passes where a few men can stop a crowd. A commander who has studied the land knows where to stand, where to hide and where a march will cost more than it can gain. The leader who is a stranger to the country he fights in has given his enemy a gift.

The fourth factor is the commander himself, who must combine wisdom, trustworthiness, kindness, courage and strictness. These qualities pull against each other, so the real skill lies in balance: too much kindness makes an army soft, and too much strictness makes it afraid. A plan is only as good as the person who has to carry it out.

The last factor, method, is the practical machinery of an army: its ranks and divisions, its rules, the roads it uses and the supplies that feed it. Courage and cunning count for little when soldiers are hungry, orders are confused or nobody knows who is in charge. Good organisation is dull to look at, but it is the quiet foundation of every victory.

Next, Sun Tzu proposes seven questions that compare the two sides, asking which ruler has the people's trust, which general is abler, and which army is better trained and more fairly rewarded and punished. He claims that from the answers he can foretell who will win, and he adds that the side which makes many calculations in advance usually triumphs while the side that makes few usually fails. The commander who has not counted at all has not made a plan, but only a wish, and wishes have never won a war.

All warfare, Sun Tzu declares, is based on deception, and a skilled commander hides the truth about his own side from the enemy. When he is strong he appears weak, when he is ready he appears careless, and when he intends to move he seems to be standing still. The enemy who believes the false picture will make his plans on a mistake, which is the greatest gift a commander can receive.

Sun Tzu offers a list of simple tricks: when you are close, appear to be far away, and when you are far, appear to be near. Dangle some bait to draw the enemy out, stir up his anger so that his judgement fails, and strike at the place where he has not prepared. These secrets of victory, he warns, cannot be explained to a general beforehand, because they depend on the moment.

In the second chapter, Sun Tzu turns from planning to the practical question of cost, and the numbers he gives are frightening. An army far from home eats, wears out its equipment and drains the treasury every day, and the farmers who feed it grow poorer with each mile it travels. A ruler who fails to count these costs may find that victory itself is more than he can afford.

Sun Tzu observes that a long campaign blunts the weapons, dampens the spirit of the soldiers and drains the strength of the state. Rival rulers, sensing the weakness, will take their chance, and no amount of cleverness can then rescue a country from the trouble it has made for itself. He knows of no case, he says, in which a country gained from a war that dragged on.

For Sun Tzu, speed is worth more than polish: a plain victory won quickly is better than an elegant one that takes years to complete. Every extra month spent in the field costs lives and money and gives the enemy time to recover, so the wise commander aims to finish the matter swiftly. This does not mean rushing without thought, but acting once the plan is ready and the moment has come.

A clever commander, Sun Tzu advises, makes the enemy's country feed his army, because hauling supplies over long roads is ruinously expensive and slow. A single wagonload of grain captured on the spot is worth many that have been carried from home, since the carrying itself eats up so much of the load. In this way an army lowers its costs while it lowers the enemy's strength as well.

Soldiers captured from the enemy, Sun Tzu says, should be treated kindly and kept, so that they may in time serve under the victor's own flags. He calls this winning a battle and growing stronger at the same time, because the conquest adds to the army instead of only subtracting from the enemy. The chapter ends with a reminder that the true aim of war is victory and not endless fighting, and that a good general holds the fate of the people in his hands.

The third chapter contains Sun Tzu's most famous idea, which is that the best victory is to take an enemy's country whole and undamaged rather than to smash it. Winning a hundred battles is not the highest skill, he says, for the highest skill is to break the enemy's will to resist without fighting at all. Destruction is expensive and leaves a mess that the winner must clean up, while a bloodless victory leaves the prize intact.

Sun Tzu ranks the possible ways of fighting in a ladder, with the best at the top and the worst at the bottom. Highest of all is to spoil the enemy's plans before they are carried out, next to separate him from his allies, then to meet his army in the field, and lowest of all to assault his walled cities. The lower the rung, the greater the cost, which is why a thoughtful commander tries to win on the upper steps.

A siege, Sun Tzu warns, is the worst of the options, because it takes months to prepare and a general who loses patience throws his men against the walls in waves. A large part of his army may be lost, and the city may still be standing at the end of it. Cities should therefore be attacked only when nothing else will do, and then only with a clear reason.

The skilled commander, in Sun Tzu's picture, subdues the enemy's army without a battle, captures his cities without a siege and ends the war without a long campaign. He takes everything under heaven whole and undamaged, so that his army is not worn down and his gain is complete. A victory of this kind makes little noise, and so it rarely makes a hero of the person who wins it.

Sun Tzu lists five signs by which a victor may be known: he knows when to fight and when to hold back, and he understands how to use both large forces and small. His ranks share a single spirit, he is prepared while his enemy is not, and he has a capable general whom the ruler does not interfere with. Where all five of these signs are present, he says, victory may be confidently expected.

A ruler, Sun Tzu warns, can bring misfortune on his own army by commanding it from far away as though it were part of his court. He may order an advance when the army ought to hold back, or a retreat when it ought to press on, and so leave his officers puzzled and distrustful. When confusion spreads through the ranks, the rival rulers come, and the army has been beaten by its own side before the enemy arrives.

Here is the line that has made the book famous: if you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, you will win some and lose some, and if you know neither, every battle will be a danger to you. The advice sounds simple, but the second half, knowing oneself honestly, is the harder task.

In the fourth chapter, on the placing of an army, Sun Tzu teaches that the skilled leader first puts himself beyond the possibility of defeat and then waits for the enemy to make himself beatable. Whether one can avoid defeat depends on one's own preparation, but whether one can win depends on the enemy's mistakes. Patience is therefore a form of strength, since no one can force a victory that the other side has not yet allowed.

Defence, Sun Tzu explains, is the right course when strength is lacking, and attack is the right course when strength is plentiful. The master of defence hides himself as if he were buried in the deepest part of the earth, while the master of attack strikes as if from the highest part of the sky. Between these two styles there is no cowardice and no boldness, only the sensible use of what one actually has.

To foresee a victory that any common person can foresee, says Sun Tzu, is not the height of skill, and to win a famous battle that the whole world applauds is not either. The truly skilled fighter wins where winning is easy, because he has already removed every difficulty, and so his victories bring neither fame nor praise. Like a man who lifts a feather and claims no strength, he has done something remarkable that looks entirely ordinary.

A victorious army, according to Sun Tzu, secures its victory first and only afterwards goes to battle, while a defeated army fights first and then looks for a way to win. The difference lies in the preparation, which is done quietly and well before a single weapon is raised. Where the preparation is thorough, the fighting is mostly a formality, and where it is missing, no amount of courage will make up for it.

The fifth chapter, on energy, begins with the observation that managing a large army is the same as managing a small one, as long as it is divided into units and given clear signals. Drums and gongs are used where the soldiers cannot see one another, and flags where they cannot hear, so that thousands may move as a single body. A crowd becomes a force only when it understands what it is being asked to do.

Sun Tzu teaches that a battle is joined by a direct method and won by an indirect one, and that the two turn into each other like a circle without an end. There are only five musical notes, he points out, and yet their combinations are more than anyone can ever hear, and the same is true of the five colours and the five tastes. In the same way, a few simple methods of fighting can be mixed to produce endless surprises.

The force of a skilled army, Sun Tzu writes, is like a rushing stream that can carry stones along with it, or like the drawn string of a crossbow that waits to be released. Energy is gathered patiently, and then, at the exact moment when it will do the most good, it is let go in one decisive burst. Like a round stone rolled down a high mountain, such an army needs only a small push, because its power was stored up beforehand.

In the sixth chapter, Sun Tzu points out that whoever occupies the field first and awaits the enemy there will be fresh, while whoever arrives second and rushes into battle will be exhausted. The skilled commander therefore draws the enemy to him and is never drawn to the enemy, so that the tired side always belongs to the other camp. In this way he controls the pace of the fight without raising his voice.

An army, Sun Tzu says, may march a great distance without tiring if it travels through country where the enemy is not. It will take what it attacks if it attacks what is not defended, and it will hold what it defends if it defends what cannot be attacked. The master of attack leaves his rival not knowing where to defend, and the master of defence leaves him not knowing where to attack.

The highest skill, Sun Tzu says, is to be formless, so that the cleverest spy cannot find a way in and the wisest enemy cannot make a plan against you. Where a commander reveals no fixed pattern, the enemy has nothing to study, and where he shows no habits, there is nothing to exploit. Mystery of this kind is not mere secrecy, but the discipline of never being predictable.

Water, Sun Tzu observes, avoids the high ground and rushes to the low, and in the same way an army avoids the strong and strikes the weak. As water shapes its course according to the ground over which it flows, so a soldier works out his victory in relation to the enemy he faces. Because there are no constant conditions in war, the commander who changes his method as the enemy changes may be called almost miraculous.

The seventh chapter, on manoeuvring, begins with the hardest problem of all, which is to turn a roundabout road into a direct one and bad luck into good. A clever commander sets out after his enemy and arrives before him, by making the enemy believe that the road is longer than it is, or by offering him something that leads him astray. In the end, skill with distance turns out to be skill with the mind of the other side.

Speed has a price, warns Sun Tzu, and an army driven on a forced march without rest arrives scattered and spent, with the strong in front and the weak far behind. Even the fastest column will perish if it has left its baggage, its food and its stores behind, since an army with no supplies is an army already half lost. The art lies in moving swiftly without breaking the very thing that is doing the moving.

Quoting an older military saying, Sun Tzu describes the ideal army by a series of images: swift as the wind, quiet as the forest, fierce as fire and unmovable as a mountain. It should be as hidden as a shadow and strike like a clap of thunder, each quality used at its proper time. The point is not to have one great virtue, but to know which one the moment demands.

Morale, Sun Tzu observes, is keenest in the morning, begins to flag by noon and is spent by the evening, and so the skilled commander avoids the enemy at his sharpest and strikes him when his spirit has sunk. He also gives a humane piece of advice, which is never to press a surrounded enemy too hard, for an opponent left without any exit will fight with the courage of despair. A way of escape, even a narrow one, therefore lowers the price of victory for the side that offers it.

The eighth chapter teaches variation in tactics, and it begins with a list of things that a wise commander will sometimes refuse to do. There are roads that should not be followed, armies that should not be attacked, cities that should not be besieged and orders from the ruler that, in the heat of events, should not be obeyed. The leader who knows these exceptions understands war, and the one who knows only the rules does not.

In planning, Sun Tzu says, the wise commander always blends considerations of advantage with considerations of disadvantage, and so keeps his thinking balanced. When he sees danger inside an opportunity, he can prepare to meet it, and when he sees an opportunity inside a difficulty, he can find a way out. Optimism and caution, used together, protect the plan from the particular weakness of each, which is why neither should ever be used alone.

Sun Tzu lists five dangerous faults in a commander: recklessness, which leads to destruction, and cowardice, which leads to capture. A hasty temper can be provoked by insults, an oversensitive pride can be wounded by shame, and an excessive concern for his men can be turned against him to make him anxious. These flaws, he says, are the ruin of an army, and a general who studies his enemy will also study himself for them.

The ninth chapter is full of practical advice for an army on the move, such as camping on high ground that faces the sun and staying close to water. Sun Tzu also teaches his officers to read the countryside: birds rising from a wood suggest hidden men, a column of dust signals an approaching force, and humble words from an enemy may mean he is about to attack. The careful observer, in other words, learns to read the whole world as a set of quiet messages.

In the tenth chapter, Sun Tzu argues that a commander who looks upon his soldiers as his own children will find them willing to follow him into the deepest valleys. Yet he adds a warning, which is that kindness without firmness produces an army of spoiled children, who cannot be used for anything that matters. Loyalty is earned by both care and discipline, and either one without the other will fail.

The eleventh chapter describes nine kinds of ground, and the most dramatic is desperate ground, where an army has no escape and must fight or perish. Place soldiers there, Sun Tzu says, and they will lose their fear, hold firm, and discover a courage that comfort would never have given them. Leaders may learn from this that people give their best when they understand that the stakes are real and that there is no retreat.

Sun Tzu praises the army that moves like a snake from a famous mountain, for when you strike its head the tail attacks, and when you strike the middle both head and tail respond. To show how common danger creates unity, he reminds us that the men of Wu and Yue, though bitter enemies, helped one another like the two hands of one body when caught in the same boat in a storm. A shared peril, in other words, can turn the bitterest rivals into partners, and a leader may use that truth to bind his army together.

The twelfth chapter treats fire as a weapon, one that can burn camps, stores, wagons and weapons, but which depends entirely on the right season and the right wind. A dry period and a rising wind are the times when fire spreads, and the commander who strikes without these conditions merely burns his own fingers. Whatever the weapon, Sun Tzu insists that it must be used at the moment when it will bring a real advantage.

No ruler should raise an army out of anger, Sun Tzu insists, and no general should fight a battle out of spite. Anger, he points out, can give way to gladness and rage can turn back into pleasure, but a ruined state can never come back into being, nor can the dead be brought to life. The enlightened ruler is cautious and the good general is watchful, and together they keep the country safe.

The final chapter is devoted to the use of spies, and it begins with the plain claim that foreknowledge cannot be had from spirits, from signs or from guesswork, but only from other people. A war costs enormous sums every day, so a ruler who refuses to pay a modest price for information, simply because he is stingy, shows a complete lack of care for those he governs. Good intelligence, in other words, is among the cheapest and most valuable things that a commander can buy.

Sun Tzu names five kinds of spies, the local ones, the inside ones, the double ones, the doomed ones and the living ones, and says that when all five are at work no one can discover the system. Of all the people in an army, none should be treated more generously or kept in more careful confidence, and no work is more secret. Only a wise and honest ruler can make use of them, and only a subtle one can learn the truth from what they report.

Two and a half thousand years later, The Art of War is still studied in military colleges and read by lawyers, athletes, business people and anyone who must compete or negotiate. Its central lesson is that careful thought, honest knowledge of oneself and one's rival, and patient preparation count for more than force, and that the finest victory is the one that leaves the battle unfought. Like any old book, it should be read with judgement, but its calm voice still has something useful to say to anyone who has a difficult contest ahead.
